title: Pygmalion in the Classroom
text:
In 1964 the psychologist Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson, a school principal, carried out a study at a public elementary school in South San Francisco, called "Oak School" in their reports. In the spring, all the children took a nonverbal intelligence test, presented to teachers as a new test that could predict which children were about to make unusual intellectual gains.

At the start of the next school year, the researchers gave each teacher the names of a few children in the class who, according to the test, were likely to "bloom" in the coming months. In reality these children, about one in five, had been picked at random. The only difference between them and their classmates was in the teachers' minds.

When the children were tested again eight months later, the "bloomers" in the first and second grades had gained noticeably more IQ points than their classmates. In the higher grades, the difference was small or absent. Teachers also described the selected children as more curious, happier and more likely to succeed. Rosenthal and Jacobson argued that teachers had treated these children differently, with more warmth, attention and encouragement, and that the children had responded. They named the effect after Pygmalion, the sculptor of Greek myth whose statue came to life.
lesson: What we expect of people can shape what they become. Make sure the people you teach, lead or raise feel that you believe in them.
source: Rosenthal, R., and Jacobson, L. (1968). Pygmalion in the Classroom: Teacher Expectation and Pupils' Intellectual Development. Holt, Rinehart and Winston.
caveat: The study was sharply criticized for its methods, and later research suggests teacher expectation effects on IQ are real but usually small.
